Course Details

Subject {L-T-P / C} : BM4203 : Surface Engineering of Biomaterials { 3-0-0 / 3}

Subject Nature : Theory

Syllabus

Module 1 :

Fundamentals of Surface Engineering
Surface-dependent engineering properties. Importance and necessity of surface engineering. Classification and scope of surface engineering in metals, ceramics, polymers, and composites. Common surface-initiated engineering failures. Mechanisms of surface degradation in materials used in the body and external environments under service conditions

Module 2 :

Surface Protection and Modification Techniques
Classification of surface modification techniques. Principles, methods, and technologies for surface engineering. Conventional surface engineering methods: Electrochemistry and electro-deposition, Thermal spraying and diffusion coatings, Chemical conversion coatings.

Module 3 :

Advanced Surface Engineering Techniques
Recent trends in surface engineering: Physical and chemical vapor deposition (PVD, CVD), Plasma spray coating, Plasma-assisted ion implantation, Surface modification using directed energy beams (ion, electron, and laser beams)
Module 4 :

Characterization and Evaluation of Surface Properties
Methods for surface characterization. Structure-property correlation in engineered surfaces. Testing and evaluation of surface performance. Case studies on different surface-modified materials.
Module 5 :

Design, Economics, and Sustainability in Surface Engineering
Economic and energy considerations in surface engineering processes. Design principles for surface engineering applications. Sustainability and environmental impact of surface modification techniques. Future trends and challenges in surface engineering

Course Objective

1 .

Understanding need of surface engineering in biomaterials
2 .

Understanding different principles of surface modification and surface engineering processes.
3 .

Understanding different methods to modify surfaces of biomaterials and choose material for desired biological response.
4 .

Understanding the application of surface engineering in medical application.

Course Outcome

1 .

The students will be able to:
1. Understand surface engineering fundamentals by explaining its importance, scope, and failure mechanisms across different materials.
2. Apply surface modification techniques by classifying, describing, and evaluating conventional and advanced methods for enhancing material performance.
3. Analyze advanced surface engineering techniques by exploring recent trends, comparing technologies, and assessing their advantages and limitations.
4. Characterize and evaluate surface properties using appropriate techniques to establish structure-property correlations and assess performance.
5. Design and optimize surface engineering processes while considering economic, energy, and sustainability factors for practical applications.

1. The students will be able to develop mathematical models of processes related to mass, heat and fluid transfer, separation and reaction using conservation principles. 2. The students will be able to analyze the dynamics of the aforesaid processes performing dynamic simulation using the MATLAB/SIMULINK environment which would help them to monitor an ongoing process and design appropriate controllers for that process to ensure product quality and process safety.

Course Details

Subject {L-T-P / C} : EE6334 : Stochastic Control Theory { 3-0-0 / 3}

Subject Nature : Theory

Syllabus

Module 1 :

Module 1: Basics of Probability, Discrete and Continuous Random Variables, Proability Mass and Density Functions, Conditional Probability, Independence. Monte Carlo simulation. (6 hours)
Module 2: Stochastic processes - Stationary and non-stationary process, Random walk, Wiener process, Gaussian process, Markov process, White noise. Discrete time system - Stochastic Difference Equation and solution, Continuous time system - Stochastic Differential Equation, basic stochastic calculus. (10 hours)
Module 3: Prediction and Optimization - State estimation for discrete time systems, Kalman - Bucy filter, Separation principle and LQG Control, Loop transfer recovery. (8 hours)
Module 4: Stochastic optimal control - Stochastic linear quadratic control, Finite horizon control, Markov chains, Markov Decision Process (MDP), Markov Reward Process (MRP), Dynamic Programming method, Value iteration, Policy iteration, Monte Carlo methods. (10 hours)
Module 5: Introduction to learning - Temporal Difference learning, SARSA, Q-Learning. (6 hours)

Course Objective

1 .

The course will provide an understanding of stochastic processes.
2 .

The course will provide an understanding of control and prediction problems under uncertainty.
3 .

The course will provide an understanding of the main results in stochastic optimal control and how they are used in various applications.

Course Outcome

1 .

At the end of the course, students will be able to
CO1: Demonstrate basic knowledge in modeling stochastic processes.
CO2: Formulate and solve prediction problems in the presence of stochasticity.
CO3: Formulate and solve stochastic optimal control problems.
CO4: Use the dynamic programming method to determine best policy under uncertainty.
CO5: Extend the ideas of stochastic control to model-free methods.
CO6: Use computational tools such as MATLAB or Python to implement the methods learned in the course.

Essential Reading

1 .

K. J. Astrom, Introduction to Stochastic Control Theory, Dover , 2004

2 .

D. Bertsekas, Dynamic programming and Optimal Control, Athena Scientific , 2007

Supplementary Reading

R. S. Sutton and A. G. Barto, Reinforcement Learning, MIT Press , 2018

19874.t: PH3101: Introduction To Condensed Matter Physics
19874.b:
Course Details

Subject {L-T-P / C} : PH3101 : Introduction To Condensed Matter Physics { 3-0-0 / 3}

Subject Nature : Theory

Syllabus

Module 1 :

(6 hrs) Structure of Condensed Matter and Bonding in solids: short and long-Range order, crystalline and non-crystalline phases, liquid phase. Cohesive energy of molecular crystal. van der Waals bonding, ionic bonding, Madelung energy, Madelung constant of NaCl. Covalent bonding, Heitler-London approximation. Brief discussion on polar covalent bond, metallic bond, Hydrogen bond.
Module 2 :

(6 hrs) Two Dimensional (2D) and Three Dimensional (3D) Lattices : Lattice, Basis, Lattice translation vector, unit cell, Crystal structure, Wigner-Seitz cell. Two and three dimensional lattice types, Symmetries in crystal, Bravais lattices and crystal Systems. Point groups and Space groups. Simple cubic, face-centered cubic, body-centered cubic, hexagonal close-packed, diamond structure.
Module 3 :

(6 hrs) Reciprocal lattice & structure determination: X-ray diffraction, Braggs law, Scattered wave amplitude Fourier analysis Reciprocal lattice vectors, Diffraction conditions, Laues Equation, Ewald construction, Miller indices. Brillouin zones (BZ), reduced and extended zone scheme, Structure and form factor. Neutron and electron diffraction (brief discussion).
Module 4 :

(10 hrs) Elastic and thermal properties of solids: Elastic strains and stress components, stiffness constants, bulk modulus, compressibility and elastic waves in cubic crystal. Harmonic and adiabatic approximation. Vibrations of a monoatomic and di-atomic linear chain. Concept of Phonons, Classical theory of specific heat, failure of classical theory. Einstein model, Debye model and Debye T3 law.
Module 5 :

(8 hrs) Electronic properties of Metals: Free electron theory: Drude model, Theory of free electron gas, ground-state energy, Fermi Dirac distribution function, Density of states, Conduction electrons, Heat Capacity of conduction electrons, DC electrical conductivity, Matthiessen’s rule, The Fermi Surface, Thermal conductivity, Wiedemann–Franz Law, Hall effect and magnetoresistance, AC conductivity and electrical properties, Thermoionc emission, Failures of the free electron model.

Course Objective

1 .

To introduce the concept of the classification of states of matter upon its degree of order and the different crystal structures along with the symmetry of the crystalline solids.
2 .

To develop the understanding of the necessity of reciprocal space and the description of diffraction conditions using the reciprocal lattice.
3 .

To provide the understanding of the mechanism of electrical and thermal properties of different materials at different conditions.
4 .

To provide the basic concept of lattice dynamics and to calculate dispersion relations for acoustical and optical phonons.
5 .

Understand the free electron theory, explore electrical and thermal transport properties, and identify the limitations of the free electron model in the case of metals.

Course Outcome

1 .

At the end of the course, students will be able to:
CO1: Classify materials based on structural order and analyze the crystal structures and symmetry of crystalline solids.
2 .

CO2: Apply reciprocal space concepts to describe diffraction conditions and analyze crystal structures using the reciprocal lattice.
3 .

CO3: Evaluate the electrical and thermal behavior of different materials.
4 .

CO4: Understand lattice dynamics and phonons in crystalline solids.
5 .

CO5: Assess the free electron model and its limitations.

C. Kittel, Introduction to Solid State Physics, John Wiley & Sons (2004).

2 .
